summary: In 1930, Pluto was found by blinking two photographs of the sky. SkyShift brings that idea to NASA's SPHEREx mission. Type a sky position (RA/Dec) and watch its SPHEREx images from 2025 to 2026 as a short time-lapse: no coding, no downloads, one link. Then SkyShift goes one step further and measures. It fits the target's motion from the SPHEREx images alone and cross-checks it against Gaia and AllWISE. For the brown dwarf Epsilon Indi B it measures 4.47 ± 0.30 arcsec per year (catalogue: 4.68). When the data is too thin, it says "not enough positions" instead of guessing. SkyShift lowers the barrier for students and citizen scientists who want to help search for moving objects such as brown dwarfs, and one day maybe Planet X. It works in English and Vietnamese, on phones and computers.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SPHEREx re-images the whole sky every six months in 102 infrared colours, so motion is already in the data, but asking "is anything moving here?" normally means writing code and downloading gigabytes. SkyShift answers it with one link. Type RA/Dec (or pick one of the five challenge targets) and it shows every SPHEREx observing epoch of that position as a flipbook, plus a difference view. Overlays add Gaia DR3 stars (moved to each frame's date), AllWISE sources at their 2010 position, and the SIMBAD object type. Every view is a shareable URL (?ra=&dec=&fov=...), and ?embed=1 gives a viewer for other websites.

HOW IT WORKS

(1) Search NASA/IPAC IRSA with SIA2 in SPHEREx Data Release 1 and Quick Release 3. (2) Group images into epochs and download small cutouts. (3) Mask flagged pixels, remove zodiacal light and background, resample onto one sky-fixed grid with each image's WCS (Astropy). (4) Median-stack each epoch and measure signal-to-noise, flux and position. (5) Fit position against time to get the proper motion. (6) Cross-check with Gaia (ESA), AllWISE (IRSA) and SIMBAD (CDS), each with a short timeout and a safe fallback.

WHAT WE FOUND (real SPHEREx data, five test targets)

The "Is it moving?" card measures motion from the images alone. The catalogue motion is not used in the fit (it only places the measurement window), so comparing the two is a real check. Epsilon Indi B: 4.47 ± 0.30 arcsec/yr from 5 positions over 515 days, catalogue 4.68, verdict Moving. Barnard's Star: 10.9 ± 2.3 against 10.39; with only 4 positions the app says Probably moving. R Draconis: no significant motion. WISE 0855 and RW Aurigae: too few measurable positions, so the app says Not enough positions. AllWISE cross-check: all five targets have a WISE source within 1.2 arcsec of their predicted 2010 position; since 2010 Barnard's Star moved 168.8 arcsec and WISE 0855 127.9 arcsec, as their known proper motions predict over about 16 years.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

We turned the blink comparator that found Pluto into a measurement. A lime arrow (measured by SPHEREx) is drawn on top of a blue arrow (catalogue), so anyone can see agreement at a glance. AllWISE diamonds stay at their 2010 positions, so a moving star sits far from its diamond: 16 years of motion in one frame. The tool also says "not enough positions" instead of inventing a number.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Honesty first: the limits are written in the app. With about one year of public data and 6.2 arcsec pixels, only motions of a few arcsec per year can be confirmed, and the uncertainty from 3-5 positions is rough. Bright stars saturate (position usable, brightness not). Each epoch sees another wavelength, so a brightness change is not proof of variability. Without a catalogue motion the measurement window does not follow the target: our blind test on Barnard's Star was inconclusive (about 6 ± 6 arcsec/yr, true 10.4). So SkyShift checks known motions; it does not claim to discover new objects or Planet X. We rejected the CatWISE catalogue because it had false motions. Outside services can go down, so the five targets are pre-computed and every overlay fails safely. English and Vietnamese, works on iPhone and Android, no NASA logos, open source (Apache-2.0).

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Students, teachers, citizen scientists and astronomers can check a target for motion in seconds, with no installation. URL parameters let other websites embed a SPHEREx time-lapse of any position. A new SPHEREx release is added with one collection name, and every new epoch makes the measurement more precise.

TOOLS AND USE OF AI

Python (Flask, NumPy, Astropy, Pillow), HTML and JavaScript, Matplotlib (slide figures), Vercel hosting. Data: NASA/IPAC IRSA (SPHEREx DR1 and QR3, AllWISE), ESA Gaia DR3, CDS SIMBAD and Sesame. AI: Claude (Anthropic) helped write the code, slides, translations and this text; ChatGPT (OpenAI) helped analyse the challenge brief and check what we had missed. We directed the work, ran every computation on real NASA data and checked each result. No image, video or audio was generated by an AI model, no simulated data was used, and no NASA branding appears. The same acknowledgement is in the GitHub README and on the last slide.
